title: Defining and cataloging variants in pangenome graphs.
data_url: https://zenodo.org/records/15374896 (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15374896; resolves to version record 15522541, 'pantree VCF generated from HPRC minigraph-cactus graphs', v1.1, licence CC BY 4.0, 8 files, 13.2 GB). Input graphs: hprc-v1.1-mc-grch38.gfa.gz and hprc-v1.1-mc-chm13.gfa.gz on the public human-pangenomics S3 bucket. Code: github.com/oclb/pantree and github.com/ShenghanZhang1123/graph_var_analysis. Supplementary tables via Europe PMC PMC13576716.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42607688, PMC13576716, open access). I downloaded the full-text XML (242,453 bytes) and read the Introduction, all Results sections, Discussion, 'Limitations of the study', 'Data and code availability', the Key resources table, the STAR Methods subsections and the full supplemental-information list. (1) Zenodo application programming interface: concept record 15374896 resolves to version record 15522541, licence CC BY 4.0, 8 files totalling 13,209,305,138 bytes - GRCh38-90.MCv1.1.vcf.gz 1,319,487,635; CHM13-90.MCv1.1.vcf.gz 1,479,369,684; GRCh38-464.MCv2.0.vcf.gz 4,883,035,608; CHM13-464.MCv2.0.vcf.gz 5,517,185,657; plus four tabix index files of 2.4-2.7 MB each. Every VCF is far over my 50 MB download rule, so I did not download any in full. (2) Zenodo serves HTTP range requests (I confirmed HTTP 206), so I pulled three slices and inflated the BGZF (block-compressed) blocks locally: 3 MB from the start of GRCh38-90.MCv1.1.vcf.gz (inflated to 50,153,162 bytes, 71,798 data rows, all chr1); 3 MB from byte offset 660,000,000 of the same file (inflated to 50,818,692 bytes, 75,210 data rows, all chr8); and 2 MB from the start of GRCh38-464.MCv2.0.vcf.gz (11,855 data rows, chr1). (3) Header, read directly: VCFv4.2, 37 meta lines = 1 fileformat + 3 FORMAT fields (GT genotype, CR reference-allele count per haplotype, CA alternative-allele count per haplotype) + 9 INFO fields (NR non-reference allele, VT variant type, DR distance from reference, RC reference-allele count, AC alternative-allele count, AN total called alleles, PV position of the variant edge's two graph nodes, TR_MOTIF tandem-repeat motif, NIA nearly-identical-alleles flag) + 24 contigs (chr1-22, X, Y). The 90-haplotype file has 55 columns = 9 fixed + 46 samples (CHM13, GRCh38 and 44 HPRC donors with 1000 Genomes identifiers such as HG00438, NA21309). The 464-haplotype file has 242 columns = 233 samples. The ID column is a graph variant edge such as '>6073185>6073183' or '<6427793<6427791'. (4) Counts I computed myself on the representative chr8 slice (75,210 rows): variant types SNP 55,266 / deletion 9,652 / insertion 8,842 / MNP 790 / replacement 660; 3,826 rows (5.1%) are non-GRCh38 (INFO NR populated); 5,105 rows (6.8%) have an empty REF column; 15,362 rows (20.4%) carry a tandem-repeat motif; 0 rows flagged nearly-identical-alleles; AN median 90, max 91, min 2; 22,623 rows (30.1%) are singletons (allele count 1); median allele frequency 0.056; the per-sample genotype field is missing ('.') in 7.22% of the 75,210 x 46 sample cells. (5) On the chr1 start slice (71,798 rows), which is the file's block of records with no linear coordinate, the picture is very different: 34,042 rows (47.4%) are non-GRCh38, 51.6% have an empty REF, and 15,344 rows (21.4%) have POS=1 together with PV=0,0 - i.e. no GRCh38 position at all, only graph node identifiers; genotype missingness there is 42.5%. (6) A cross-tabulation I ran confirms the trap the authors warn about in the Discussion: an empty REF column does NOT mean 'non-GRCh38'. In the chr8 slice, 1,279 of 75,210 rows have an empty REF with INFO NR unset - these are ordinary insertions on the linear reference - while 3,826 have an empty REF with NR set. You must read NR and VT together. (7) Decisive check: neither the 90-haplotype nor the 464-haplotype deposited VCF contains any CHM13 haplotype-position field. The INFO list is the same 9 fields in both. The paper's only functional annotation (which gene, exon or coding sequence a non-GRCh38 variant falls in) was computed from a different, haplotype-contiguous-tree VCF carrying those positions, and that file is not in the deposit. (8) Europe PMC supplementary bundle: 5,761,294 bytes, 22 files (19 .xlsx + 3 .pdf). I opened all 19 spreadsheets with openpyxl. Every one is an aggregate summary, not a per-variant table; row counts are S1=3, S2=24, S3=10, S4=5, S5=10, S6=5, S7=185, S8=185, S9=185, S10=70, S11=93, S12=8, S13=3, S14=8, S15=6,499, S16=5, S17=25, S18=26, S19=5. (9) Numbers I recomputed from those tables: Table S7's genome-wide 'Total' row gives 29,334,746 variants on chr1-22, of which 25,946,412 on-GRCh38 and 3,388,334 (11.55%) non-GRCh38; Table S2's 23 chromosome rows sum to exactly 3,453,855, matching Table S1. Table S18 records pantree's own resource use: 26.4-34.4 GB peak memory and 3.1-6.7 hours per chromosome. Table S4 holds the HG002 chromosome-21 vcfeval benchmark: SNP false negatives / false positives and indel false negatives / false positives for raw (106/3,038/122/331), vcfwave (379/409/303/449), pantree (691/357/1,885/858) and pantree-pairwise (180/550/138/378). (10) HTTP HEAD on the input graphs: hprc-v1.1-mc-grch38.gfa.gz is 9,039,449,789 bytes and hprc-v1.1-mc-chm13.gfa.gz is 9,473,687,712 bytes. (11) GitHub application programming interface on oclb/pantree: Python, 33 stars, and license reported as null; I listed the repository root and there is no LICENSE file, so the software the paper calls 'open-source' is publicly readable but formally unlicensed. The VCF data on Zenodo is separately and clearly CC BY 4.0.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: I did not count the rows of any VCF - that needs streaming roughly 22 GB of uncompressed text for the smallest file. My estimate from compressed bytes per row (about 40 compressed bytes per record in both slices) is roughly 33 million records in GRCh38-90.MCv1.1.vcf.gz across chr1-22 plus X and Y, which is the right order of magnitude for the published 29,334,746 autosomal records plus the sex chromosomes, but it is an estimate, not a count. Taken from the text and not verifiable in the deposit: the headline 29.6 million variants and 3.5 million (11.7%) non-GRCh38 variants; 129.3 megabases of non-GRCh38 sequence in the graph; 99.2% of variants being small (<50 bp combined allele length); 21,109 variants that are both common and large; 14,562 non-GRCh38 variants overlapping coding sequence in 1,182 genes including HLA, immunoglobulin, KIR, HTT, ATXN1, ATXN2 and ATXN3; the 90% cross-graph recovery rate for 7,754 chromosome-21 non-GRCh38 variants between the year-1 and year-2 graphs; and the HLA-A and RHD locus analyses. I did not open mmc1.pdf (Document S1, Figures S1-S16, 1,344,289 bytes), mmc21.pdf or mmc22.pdf. I did not download the 9 GB pangenome graphs, did not run pantree, vg, vcfwave or RTG vcfeval, and did not retrieve the full text of any of the prior-work papers listed in the C2 audit - for those I read only search-result titles and summaries.

a1_downloadable.note: Passes. The Zenodo record is fully open with no login and no access application, licensed CC BY 4.0, and the server honours HTTP range requests so even the multi-gigabyte files can be sampled politely. The input graphs sit on a public S3 bucket. Two frictions, not failures: every VCF (1.3-5.5 GB) exceeds my 50 MB download rule, and the pantree code repository has no LICENSE file despite the paper calling it open-source.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS, and this is the decisive one. I read the complete INFO and FORMAT field list straight out of the file header: 9 INFO fields and 3 FORMAT fields, every one of which describes the variant's own representation in the graph (variant type, allele counts, node positions, tandem-repeat motif, nearly-identical-alleles flag) or the genotypes of the 44 assembly donors. There is no measured outcome anywhere - no pathogenicity, no expression effect, no function, no validation status. Any target worth predicting would have to be built by joining to an outside resource, and for the paper's headline 3.5 million non-GRCh38 variants that join is impossible from the deposit: the CHM13 haplotype positions the authors themselves used to work out which gene a non-reference variant hits are not in either deposited VCF, and a substantial block of these records (15,344 of 34,042 in my chr1 slice) carries POS=1 and PV=0,0, meaning no genomic coordinate at all. This is a variant-discovery catalog, which is exactly what the authors say it is - the Discussion states plainly that 'the functional consequences of the genetic variants that we found are unknown.'

a3_inputs_present.note: FAILS for every framing with a real biological question behind it. The file gives you the allele strings but no flanking sequence context, which is what any DNA model needs. For on-GRCh38 records you could pull context from a reference FASTA, but for the non-GRCh38 records - the entire novelty here - the context lives only in the pangenome graph, so the input is a pair of graph node identifiers pointing into a 9.0 GB compressed GFA file (roughly 30 GB uncompressed) whose node numbering is specific to one graph build.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes. Nothing here is a physical quantity needing units: everything is a count, a category or a coordinate, and the header documents each one. The denominators are explicit too (AN, the number of called alleles, which I confirmed is 90 or 91 in the 90-haplotype file). One recorded trap: coordinates are meaningless without the genome build and the graph version, and the same variant has different node identifiers in the year-1 and year-2 graphs.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS, in the 'huge number, no labelled examples' way. I did not count rows (that needs streaming 22 GB); the published figure is 29,334,746 records on chr1-22 from Table S7, which I verified as the table's own total. But zero of those rows carry a label, so the number of labelled examples is nil. And the unit that governs any population-level question is the donor: 44 HPRC individuals in the year-1 graph, 233 in the year-2 graph. For allele-frequency work the resolution is 90 haplotypes, in which 30.1% of variants are singletons - a very coarse and noisy outcome.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 1.32 GB compressed / about 22 GB uncompressed for the smallest single VCF; 13.2 GB compressed / well over 100 GB uncompressed for the whole deposit; plus 9.0 GB compressed for the GRCh38 pangenome graph if you need sequence context
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS on the checklist's ~5 GB working-set limit. A streaming, chromosome-at-a-time pass to build a features-only table keeps peak memory near 2 GB, so it is not impossible, but the data you must move is 22 GB minimum and 30+ GB more if you need the graph. Regenerating the haplotype-position annotations the paper used is flatly out of reach: the authors' own Table S18 records 26.4-34.4 GB peak memory and 3.1-6.7 hours per chromosome for pantree. Embedding millions of sites with a DNA language model on a CPU is also not laptop work (see effort).

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Passes, after I chased down what looked like a contradiction. Table S7's own genome-wide total is 29,334,746 variants on chr1-22 with 3,388,334 (11.55%) non-GRCh38, against the abstract's 29.6 million and 3.5 million (11.7%) - the gap is the sex chromosomes. Table S1's 44,022,198 'on-GRCh38 variants' looked inconsistent until the Methods made clear it comes from the year-2 (464-haplotype) graph, not the year-1 graph the abstract describes. Table S2's 23 chromosome rows sum to exactly 3,453,855, matching Table S1. My own byte-per-record estimate of about 33 million records in the year-1 GRCh38 file is consistent in magnitude. Everything reconciles once you track which graph each number came from, which the tables do not always say.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS for every candidate label the file actually offers. The obvious ones - 'is this variant non-GRCh38?', 'what type of variant is it?', 'is it in a tandem repeat?' - are all deterministic functions of the record itself, computed by pantree from the graph topology. Predicting them is leakage by construction; I verified the non-GRCh38 flag is literally readable from whether the INFO NR field is populated. The only remaining candidate, allele count, is computed from the genotype columns that sit in the same row. And every record ultimately derives from the Minigraph-Cactus graph, which is itself the output of an alignment pipeline, so even the variant set is a tool's output rather than a measurement - the authors say as much, warning that their variants 'should not be interpreted as a record of individual mutation events'.

existing_models.name: PanGenie (Ebler et al., Nature Genetics 2022) - a genotyper that counts short DNA words (k-mers) in a new person's sequencing reads and uses a haplotype-resolved pangenome to call their genotypes without aligning to a graph
existing_models.score_and_split: From the search-result summary only: more than 4 times faster than mapping-based approaches at 30-fold coverage, with better genotype concordance for almost all variant types and coverages tested. I did not retrieve the paper or verify any number, and I did not run it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved verbatim. This paper's own Discussion names the gap from its side: 'A natural question, having discovered variants in a pangenome graph, is how to genotype these variants in a new sample not belonging to the graph. pantree is not designed for this problem', and suggests PanGenie could in principle be modified to take a pantree VCF as input.

existing_models.name: vg giraffe - the open-source pangenome read mapper in the vg toolkit, with a 2025 preprint extending it to long reads
existing_models.score_and_split: From the search-result summary only: mapping to a pangenome holding more than 450 human haplotypes is comparable in speed to linear mappers, for both short and long reads. No accuracy number retrieved and nothing run.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved. This paper nominates giraffe as 'one possible but suboptimal approach' to genotyping pantree variant edges from read support.

existing_models.name: Pangenome-aware DeepVariant (released June 2025) - a convolutional neural network small-variant caller that takes pangenome context as an extra input channel
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved. I saw only a search-result summary saying it exists and improves small-variant calling; DeepVariant itself is open source. No number, no split, nothing run.

existing_models.name: Evo 2 (Nature 2026) - a genomic foundation model trained on 9 trillion DNA bases that scores the functional impact of any nucleotide change without task-specific training
existing_models.score_and_split: From the search-result summary only: described as the current state of the art for zero-shot variant scoring, and notable here because its autoregressive objective scores any sequence, reference or non-reference. No number verified, nothing run.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved. The same summaries note that specialist tools such as AlphaMissense still lead on coding single-nucleotide pathogenicity, which is an implicit statement of what is unsolved.

existing_models.name: AlphaGenome (2026) - a deep learning model predicting 5,930 human functional genomic signals from up to one million bases of DNA
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond search-result summaries describing it as leading on noncoding and splice variant effect. Weights are non-commercial. Important limitation for this dataset: it is anchored on reference-genome coordinates, so it cannot score the non-GRCh38 variants that are the whole point of this paper without first reconstructing their sequence from the graph.

existing_models.name: Machine learning-based prediction of human structural variation and characterization of associated sequence determinants (bioRxiv 2025 / PMC12710826) - a convolutional network on raw sequence plus a random forest on genomic annotations, predicting where structural variants occur
existing_models.score_and_split: From the search-result summary only: each model alone exceeds 90% area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve, improved further in an ensemble, and the predicted probability correlates with allele frequency and gene functional constraint. Split not retrieved. This is the closest published analogue to the 'predict variant presence or frequency from sequence' framing I considered.

existing_models.name: Varigraph (2025) - a pangenome-graph-based genotyper for diploid and polyploid genomes
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved as a title and summary only; described as accurate and widely applicable. No number, nothing run.

existing_models.name: A supervised model trained on a pangenome variant catalog itself (predicting anything about pantree-style variant edges)
existing_models.score_and_split: I found none in four searches, so call this likely absent. But the absence has an obvious cause rather than being an opening: there is nothing to supervise on. The field's effort is going into genotyping these variants in new people (PanGenie, giraffe, pangenome-aware DeepVariant, Varigraph) and into scoring variant effects from sequence (Evo 2, AlphaGenome), both of which need data this deposit does not contain.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: This paper's own closing sentence is the clearest statement of the open problem: 'The functional consequences of the genetic variants that we found are unknown... Understanding the effects of such variants at these and other loci will require experimental evidence and, possibly, genetic association studies.' That is a call for wet-lab and cohort work, not for a model.

backbone.name: A DNA language model would be the right family - Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA have open weights and small checkpoints, and Evo 2 is the strongest zero-shot variant scorer - but none of them can be applied to this deposit as it stands, because the VCF carries allele strings without flanking sequence and the non-GRCh38 records have no coordinate from which to fetch context. You would first have to extract windows from the 9.0 GB compressed pangenome graph.
backbone.hardware: Not laptop-feasible at the scale of the data. Embedding even the 3.4 million non-GRCh38 sites with a small DNA model on a 16 GB central processing unit, at an optimistic 5 windows per second, is about 190 hours. There is also no label to attach a head to, so 'freeze and head' has nothing to train on.
backbone.licence: Mixed, and mostly fine: the VCF deposit is CC BY 4.0, the HPRC graphs are open, and Nucleotide Transformer / DNABERT-2 / HyenaDNA weights are permissive. Two flags: AlphaGenome weights are non-commercial, and the pantree repository has no LICENSE file at all (GitHub reports no licence), so the software is public but formally all-rights-reserved.

integration.partner_dataset: gnomAD v4 (population allele frequencies for hundreds of thousands of people, keyed on GRCh38 coordinates), ClinVar (clinical interpretations, same key), and the 1000 Genomes Project panel - the 44 and 233 donor identifiers in the VCF are 1000 Genomes sample identifiers (HG00438, NA21309 and so on), so population and superpopulation labels join cleanly.
integration.join_key: GRCh38 chromosome and position for the on-GRCh38 records, which is a proper standard identifier; 1000 Genomes sample identifiers for the donor columns. But the join fails exactly where the paper is interesting: non-GRCh38 variants have an empty REF, and a large share of them (I counted 15,344 of 34,042 in my chr1 slice) have POS=1 with PV=0,0, so they have no coordinate to join on, and the CHM13 haplotype positions that would give them one are not in the deposited files.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the variants that only a pangenome can see show the same population-frequency structure and the same depletion of function-altering alleles as the variants we already see on the linear reference, and are they enriched in medically relevant loci? That is a genuinely good question that neither dataset answers alone, but it is a population-genetics comparison rather than a prediction task, and the deposit is missing the one annotation (which gene a non-reference variant hits) needed to run the interesting half of it.

controls.positive_control: Good ones exist for a pipeline, which is the frustrating part. Non-GRCh38 variants must come out enriched in segmental duplications and in the HLA region - the paper shows this and supplementary Table S9 gives the per-chromosome breakdown to check against. The HG002 Q100 small-variant truth set is a genuine external benchmark, and supplementary Table S4 gives the published false-positive and false-negative counts on chromosome 21 to reproduce. None of these control a model, because there is no model to control.
controls.negative_control: Would be straightforward if there were a label: shuffle it and confirm collapse to the majority class (which for variant type is already 71% single-nucleotide polymorphisms in my chr8 slice), and hold out whole chromosomes or whole superbubbles rather than single records, since adjacent variant edges inside one superbubble are heavily correlated and a random split would leak outright.
controls.external_validation: Unusually well supplied: the CHM13-aligned VCFs are the same variants called against a different reference, the year-2 (464-haplotype) graph is an independently constructed graph with a published 90% cross-graph recovery rate for non-GRCh38 variants, and HG002 is a sample absent from the year-1 graph with a manually curated truth set. The evaluation machinery is not the problem here; the missing label is.

honest_claim_h3: The most a model built on what is actually deposited could honestly claim is: 'given the allele strings, allele counts and graph-topology annotations that pantree already wrote into this VCF for the 44 Human Pangenome Reference Consortium assemblies in the year-1 Minigraph-Cactus graph, this reproduces another annotation that pantree computed from the same graph.' That is a statement about one software tool's bookkeeping, not about human genetic variation.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use local DNA sequence to predict how often a variant that only a multi-genome reference can see appears across human haplotypes.
plain_idea.train_on: What the model would see for each example: a window of DNA sequence around a variant site, plus simple annotations such as whether the site sits in a repeat or a duplicated region. The catalog holds about 29.3 million variant records on chromosomes 1-22 (a number I recomputed from the paper's own summary table, not by counting the file), of which about 3.4 million are the non-reference ones that are the paper's novelty. But the sequence window is not in the deposited files - it would have to be cut out of a 9 gigabyte compressed graph file.
plain_idea.predict: How many of the 90 human haplotypes in the graph carry the variant - an integer from 1 to 89. The true answer is not a measurement: it is counted off the genome assemblies of 44 donors after an alignment program decided which of their sequences correspond to each other, and 30% of variants are seen in exactly one haplotype.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Human geneticists and clinical sequencing labs genuinely need to know whether the variation hidden in non-reference sequence behaves like ordinary variation, because that decides whether pangenome references are worth adopting for diagnosis. But answering it needs frequencies from a large cohort and functional annotation, neither of which is in this release.

ml_idea: Three framings, and all three die on the files. (1) Predict a variant's population frequency, or whether it exists at all, from local DNA sequence. The label (allele count out of 90) is a column, but the input is not: the VCF stores allele strings with no flanking context, and for the 3.4 million non-GRCh38 records there is no coordinate from which to fetch context, only a pair of graph node identifiers pointing into a 9.0 GB compressed GFA. The label is also extremely coarse - 44 donors, 30% singletons - and a published model already does the sequence-to-structural-variant version at over 90% area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve. (2) Predict which variants are real, reproducible or clinically meaningful. There is no such column anywhere. The paper's own cross-graph reproducibility result (90% of 7,754 chromosome-21 non-GRCh38 variants recovered) and its HG002 benchmark exist only as aggregate counts in supplementary Tables S6 and S4, five rows each - not as a per-variant flag. Building a per-variant version means re-running pantree on both 9 GB graphs, which the authors' own Table S18 says costs 26-34 GB of memory and 3-7 hours per chromosome. (3) Predict the functional consequence of non-reference variants. This is the question the paper actually raises, and its Discussion says outright that these consequences 'are unknown'. The decisive thing I verified: the deposited VCFs do not carry the CHM13 haplotype positions the authors used for their own gene-overlap analysis - I read the INFO field list in both the 90- and the 464-haplotype file and it is the same 9 fields, with no haplotype-position field - so you cannot even reproduce which gene a non-reference variant hits, let alone join to ClinVar or gnomAD. Two findings worth reporting rather than modelling: the deposit's VCFs are missing the haplotype positions needed for the paper's Figure 5 analysis, so that result is not reproducible from the release; and an empty REF column does not mean 'non-GRCh38' (I found 1,279 of 75,210 chr8 rows with an empty REF and no NR field - ordinary insertions), a trap the authors do flag in the Discussion but which will silently corrupt anyone's first pass. This is an excellent and well-documented resource for the people building pangenome genotypers. It is not a supervised learning dataset.

effort.compute_note: All sizes are from files I touched: the Zenodo application programming interface gave exact byte counts, and two 3 MB range requests told me the uncompressed cost (about 40 compressed and 676 uncompressed bytes per record, so 22 GB uncompressed for the 1.32 GB year-1 GRCh38 file). peak_ram_gb of 2 assumes the obvious streaming route, one chromosome at a time; regenerating the paper's haplotype-position annotations instead needs 26-34 GB by the authors' own Table S18, which no laptop has. embedding_hours is 3.4 million non-reference sites at an optimistic 5 windows per second on a central processing unit; nothing was timed. hours_to_feature_table is dominated by moving 22 GB and by writing careful code for the empty-REF / NR convention, not by modelling.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Range-request the first 100 kilobytes of any deposited VCF and read the header's INFO and FORMAT field list. It takes five minutes, and it tells you two fatal things at once: there is no outcome column of any kind, and there is no CHM13 haplotype position, so non-reference variants cannot be mapped to a gene or joined to any annotation database. The second-cheapest check is to count how many records have POS=1 - those have no genomic coordinate at all.

verdict_reason: This is a variant-definition and discovery resource, not a modelling dataset, and it fails Part A at four of the eight killers - all checked by range-reading the actual files, not inferred from the abstract. A2 is the decisive failure: I read the complete header of both deposited VCFs and found 9 INFO fields and 3 FORMAT fields, every one of which is pantree's own description of how a variant sits in the graph (type, allele counts, node positions, tandem-repeat motif) plus the genotypes of 44 or 233 assembly donors. There is no measured outcome anywhere, and the authors say so themselves: 'the functional consequences of the genetic variants that we found are unknown.' The one thing that could anchor a biological label - which gene a non-reference variant hits - cannot even be reconstructed, because the CHM13 haplotype positions the authors used for their own coding-sequence analysis are absent from both deposited files (same 9 INFO fields in the 90- and the 464-haplotype VCF), and a large block of non-GRCh38 records carries POS=1 with PV=0,0, meaning no genomic coordinate at all (15,344 of 34,042 in my chr1 slice). A8 compounds it: every label the file does offer - the non-GRCh38 flag, the variant type, the repeat annotation - is a deterministic function of the same record, computed by the same program from the same graph, so predicting it is leakage by construction. A3 fails because the inputs a DNA model needs are not here: allele strings are present but flanking sequence is not, and for the non-reference variants the only pointer to context is a pair of node identifiers into a 9.0 GB compressed graph. A6 fails on the size filter: 13.2 GB of compressed VCF in the deposit, 22 GB uncompressed for the smallest single file, 9 GB more for the graph, and the authors' Table S18 records 26-34 GB peak memory and 3-7 hours per chromosome for the tool itself. A5 fails in the 'huge number, no labelled examples' way - 29.3 million records that I confirmed as Table S7's own total, zero of them labelled, and only 44 donors behind the year-1 catalog with 30% of variants seen in a single haplotype. To the authors' real credit, A1, A4 and A7 pass cleanly and the resource is unusually well made: fully open on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, range-request friendly, tabix-indexed, every field documented in the header, no units ambiguity, and the counts reconcile once you track which graph each number came from (Table S7's 29,334,746 autosomal records versus the abstract's 29.6 million is the sex chromosomes; Table S1's 44 million is the year-2 graph; Table S2 sums to exactly Table S1's 3,453,855). The evaluation machinery a project would want is also excellent and sitting right there - a CHM13-aligned callset as a second reference, an independently built year-2 graph with a published 90% recovery rate, and the HG002 Q100 truth set with published false-positive and false-negative counts in Table S4. None of that rescues it, because what is missing is the label, and the field's own effort is pointed elsewhere: PanGenie, vg giraffe, pangenome-aware DeepVariant and Varigraph are all working on genotyping these variants in new people, while Evo 2 and AlphaGenome score variant effects from sequence. Scoring stopped at Part A, so score_items is empty by design; that is not a judgement on B through J. Two findings worth sending to the authors: the deposited VCFs lack the haplotype positions needed to reproduce their own Figure 5 gene-overlap analysis, and an empty REF column does not mean 'non-GRCh38' (1,279 of 75,210 chromosome-8 rows are ordinary insertions with an empty REF), a trap they flag in the Discussion but which will silently corrupt anyone's first pass over the file.
